opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, when I first heard Eliahu frame it that way, weights as a modality in their own right, it really resonated, because it's essentially the idea we've been circling around in our group for a few years now. We usually think of modalities as images, text, audio, maybe graphs or tabular data. But if you step back, a trained neural network's weights are also data. They're a very rich, structured artifact. They encode what the model learned, how it was trained, what data it saw, and to some extent how well it will generalize. So the question becomes: why not learn from them directly?

What I recognized was the shift in perspective. For a long time, the weights were just the byproduct of training. You train a model, you deploy it, and nobody really looks at the parameters themselves except maybe for pruning or quantization. But we now have this enormous and growing population of models, on Hugging Face and in companies' internal repositories, and that population starts to look like a dataset. Once you have that, you can ask the same questions you'd ask of any other modality: can we learn representations of these objects, can we classify them, can we predict their properties, can we even generate new ones?

That's very much where our work on model zoos and what we've called hyper-representations came from. We trained populations of models in a controlled way and then trained models on those weights, for example to predict accuracy or hyperparameters, or to reconstruct and sample new weights. Seeing someone else independently arrive at the framing of "this is a new modality" was really encouraging, because it tells you the community is converging on the idea.

And it also reminded me of the specific challenges that make this modality different. Weights have these symmetries. You can permute neurons in a layer and get exactly the same function. So two networks can look completely different in parameter space and be functionally identical. Then there's the scale, models with billions of parameters, and the heterogeneity, because architectures differ. Images all live on a pixel grid. Weights don't have such a convenient common structure. So I think recognizing weights as a modality is the first step, and the interesting research is in figuring out the right inductive biases and architectures to actually handle them.

r001.rationale: The response says that others independently arrived at the same framing and that this shows the community is converging on viewing weights as a modality.

fable-5.1.text:
What I recognized, honestly, was our own motivation. When Eliahu framed weights as a modality, it put a name on something we'd been circling for years. If you look at Hugging Face right now, there are over a million models sitting there, and each of those weight files is the result of an enormous amount of compute and data. That's an artifact. It carries information about what the model learned, how it was trained, what data it saw, maybe even what biases it inherited. And yet we treat it as a black box. We don't inspect it the way we inspect images or text.

Our group had been working on this from a very concrete angle. We asked a simple question: if I give you only the weights of a trained network, nothing else, can you tell me something about it? Can you tell me its test accuracy, what optimizer was used, what dataset it was trained on, whether it's been fine-tuned or poisoned? And it turned out that you can, often surprisingly well. We built what we called model zoos, thousands of small networks trained under controlled variations, so we could study this systematically. And then the next step was hyper-representations, learning an embedding of weight space itself so you could not only predict properties but also generate new weights, sample initializations, do model editing in that latent space.

So when Eliahu described the weights as a new data type with its own structure, its own symmetries, its own need for dedicated architectures, I thought, yes, this is exactly the framing. The permutation symmetry alone makes it hard. You can shuffle neurons in a layer and get a functionally identical network with a completely different weight vector. That's a fundamental difference from images or language, and it means you can't just throw a transformer at the flattened parameters and hope. You need equivariant architectures, or clever canonicalization, or augmentation strategies that respect those symmetries.

What I also recognized was the shared sense that this is still early. We're where computer vision was before ImageNet, in a way. We have the data, millions of models, but we're still figuring out the right representations and the right benchmarks. His framing of it as a modality helps the community realize there's a field here, not just a scattering of curiosities.

r001.rationale: The response says Eliahu’s framing matched the group’s existing work and describes a shared sense that weights have their own structure and need dedicated methods, conveying researchers’ convergence on weights as a new modality.

astra-6.text:
What I recognized was a shift in perspective that is very close to how we think about learning from neural network weights. Usually, the weights are the result of learning: you train a network, and then you use it to make predictions. But you can also treat those weights as data. If you have a collection of trained networks, can you learn something from that collection?

That’s what makes the idea of a new modality interesting. The weights contain information about what a model has learned, but accessing that information is challenging. Two networks can implement the same function while having very different weight representations—for example, because their neurons are ordered differently. So the question becomes: how do we build representations of weights that capture meaningful differences between models while accounting for those symmetries?

r001.rationale: The response describes treating trained-network weights as data and says the idea is interesting, but it does not identify a convergence among researchers on this view.

sol-6.1.text:
What resonated with me was the idea that the weights themselves are data. We usually look at a neural network as a function: you give it an input and inspect its output. But you can also look inside and ask what the parameters tell you about what that network has learned.

Calling that a new modality captures a shift in perspective. Instead of learning from images or text, you learn from trained models. Then the question becomes: how do you represent those weights so you can compare networks and extract useful information from them?

r001.rationale: The response describes neural-network weights as data and calls them a new modality, but it does not say that researchers are converging on this view.
